keywords: Corn / maize maizium, maiziī n. Neo-Latin Stem quantity uncertain maizium, maiziī n. — maize; recorded in Morgan–Owens. keywords: Vitamin vītamīnum, vītamīnī n. Neo-Latin Reading convention vītamīnum, vītamīnī n. — vitamin; a modern lexical form. The feminine variant vitamina, vitaminae f. is also recorded by Morgan–Owens, without documented stem quantities. vītamīna, vītamīnōrum n. pl. — vitamins, using the neuter form. vītamīnicus, vītamīnica, vītamīnicum — pertaining to vitamins; a transparent derivative, not claimed here to be corpus-verified. For a multivitamin preparation, praeparātum plūra vītamīna continēns is an explicit description; the previous unsupported claim for multivītamīnum has been withdrawn. Hic cibus multa vītamīna continet. — This food contains many vitamins. The international term was coined from “vita” and “amine”; it does not imply that all vitamins are amines. The ī in vīta and the adopted international -amīn- reading give our convention vītamīnum ; these are reconstructed Neo-Latin reading quantities, not attested Classical measurements.

keywords: Pea / bean / lentil / chickpea / pulses pīsum, pīsī n. · phasēlus, phasēlī m. Ancient Latin pīsum, pīsī n. — pea (Bulg. грах); Columella II 10, 4; Plīn. NH XVIII 123. Lewis & Short marks the ī long (late collateral pīsa, pīsae f.), and French pois continues the long vowel. pīsa viridia — green peas, our phrase for the shelled table vegetable. phasēlus, phasēlī m. — the pod bean (Bulg. фасул, боб); Verg. G. I 227 (vīlemque phasēlum); Columella X 377. The modern green and kidney beans are an American species that inherited the ancient name (Phaseolus vulgaris, Linn.); Ep. VII uses phasēlī of Baba’s garden. faba, fabae f. — the broad bean, the ancient staple bean (Bulg. бакла); Catō Agr. 35, 1; Plīn. NH XVIII 117. In the market stores of Ep. IV. lēns, lentis f. — lentil (Bulg. леща); Plīn. NH XVIII 123; Catō writes the accusative lentim (Agr. 35). Also Ep. IV. cicer, ciceris n. — chickpea (Bulg. нахут); Hor. S. I 6, 115 (ad porrī et ciceris … catīnum); the cēna rūstica of Ep. III. siliqua, siliquae f. — pod (Bulg. шушулка); Varr. RR I 23, 3; Verg. G. I 74. The plural siliquae is pulse in general (Hor. Ep. II 1, 123). legūmen, legūminis n. — any pulse or leguminous plant; Cic. ND II 156; already the Ep. III gloss for cicer. Pīsa ē siliquīs exprimāmus. — Let’s pop the peas out of their pods. Jūs ē phasēlīs coquitur. — Bean soup is cooking (Bulg. бобена чорба). The bean words divide cleanly: faba is the ancient broad bean, phasēlus the pod bean whose name the American Phaseolus inherited, pīsum the pea. All quantities follow Lewis & Short.

english: Onion / leek / cabbage / sauerkraut / courgette / eggplant / potato
latin: caepa, caepae f. · brassica, brassicae f.
keywords: Onion / leek / cabbage / sauerkraut / courgette / eggplant / potato caepa, caepae f. · brassica, brassicae f. Ancient words Modern species caepa, caepae f. — onion (Bulg. лук); also spelled cēpa, with a neuter by-form caepe; the series’ spelling is caepa (Ep. VII). porrum, porrī n. — leek (Bulg. праз); Plīn. NH XIX 108; Horace’s supper of leeks and chickpeas, S. I 6, 115. brassica, brassicae f. — cabbage (Bulg. зеле); Catō Agr. 156, 1: brassica est quae omnibus holeribus antistat (ūsus: Ep. III, Culīna). brassica muriā condīta — sauerkraut (Bulg. кисело зеле), our phrase after Catō’s brined olives (Agr. 7, 4: conduntur … viridēs in muriā). cucurbitula, cucurbitulae f. — courgette, zucchini (Bulg. тиквичка); the Culīna’s diminutive of cucurbita. The attested classical senses are a wild gourd and Celsus’s cupping-glass (Cels. II 11), so the vegetable sense is our extension. melongēna, melongēnae f. — eggplant, aubergine (Bulg. патладжан); a medieval word from Arabic, kept in the botanical name Solanum melongena; Ep. VI (pitta cum melongēnīs). pōmum terrestre; pōma terrestria — potato; potatoes (Bulg. картофи); Traupman 72, whose pulticula ex pōmīs terrestribus is mashed potatoes (ūsus: Culīna). piperītis, piperītidis f. — the fresh pepper (Bulg. чушка); in Plīn. NH XX 174 a pepperwort; Traupman 71 applies it to the fresh Capsicum, and the series follows him (Epp. VI–VII). See the Red pepper entry for capsicum, and the pepper spice under piper. Baba in hortō phasēlōs, caepās, cucumerēs colit. — Baba grows beans, onions and cucumbers in the garden (after Ep. VII). cf. Vulg. Num. 11, 5, where Israel remembers the cucumerēs, pepōnēs, porrī and cēpae of Egypt (cited at Lewis & Short, pepo). The potato, the eggplant and the sweet pepper are modern crops wearing borrowed names.

english: Cherry / peach / apricot / quince / melon / watermelon / chestnut
latin: cerasum, cerasī n. · Persicum, Persicī n.
keywords: Cherry / peach / apricot / quince / melon / watermelon / chestnut cerasum, cerasī n. · Persicum, Persicī n. Ancient words Modern species cerasum, cerasī n. — cherry (Bulg. череша); Cels. II 24. The tree is cerasus, cerasī f., which Lucullus brought to Italy from Cerasūs in Pontus (Plīn. NH XV 102; Varr. RR I 39, 2) — a name-story that can be told as true. Persicum, Persicī n. — peach (Bulg. праскова), the “Persian apple” (mālum Persicum); Plīn. NH XV 42; Mart. XIII 46. The tree is Persica, Persicae f. Armeniacum, Armeniacī n. — apricot (Bulg. кайсия), the “Armenian apple” (mālum Armeniacum); Columella V 10, 19. The tree is Armeniaca (Plīn. NH XV 41). cydōnium, cydōniī n.; pl. cydōnia — quince (Bulg. дюля), mālum cydōnium, the apple of Cydōnia in Crete; Varr. RR I 59; Plīn. NH XV 37; the Latinized spelling is cotōnea. pepō, peponis m. — sweet melon (Bulg. пъпеш); Plīn. NH XIX 65; Vulg. Num. 11, 5. The Greek oblique stem (πέπων, -ονος) keeps its o short. mēlopepō, mēlopeponis m. — the apple-shaped melon of Plīn. NH XIX 67; shortened late to mēlo, mēlōnis m. (Pallad. IV 9, 6), the ancestor of the modern melon-words. citrullus, citrullī m. — watermelon (Bulg. диня); not ancient — a medieval word kept in the botanical name Citrullus lanatus. Stem quantities are conventional, not attested. castanea, castaneae f. — chestnut (Bulg. кестен); Verg. Ecl. II 52 (castaneāsque nucēs); roasted as castaneae tostae in the Culīna, after the Conimbriga market of Ep. IV. Cerasa Jūniō mātūrēscunt, Persica Augustō. — Cherries ripen in June, peaches in August. All the orchard words but citrullus are ancient. Lewis & Short prints pepo, -ŏnis but mēlopepo, -ōnis; the shared Greek stem πέπων, -ονος settles both short, and the entries above follow the Greek.
